story.title: Netanyahu Accused of Smearing Arab Parties After Election Loss
story.summary: Following the recent elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics against Arab Israeli parties, alleging they received foreign support to 'steal' the election. His coalition lost its parliamentary majority, prompting calls for investigations into alleged vote buying. As opposition parties begin coalition negotiations, Netanyahu's claims have sparked accusations of attempting to delegitimize the election results.

timeline_highlights.title: Netanyahu's Bloc Leads Israeli Election, But Majority Remains Elusive
timeline_highlights.summary: As of the latest counts, Netanyahu's right-wing bloc is leading the Israeli election but is falling short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset. With over 85% of the votes counted, projections indicate that Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies are set to secure around 53 seats, while the opposing coalition led by Eisenkot is expected to gain approximately 48 seats, alongside 19 seats for Arab-led parties. The results suggest a potential deadlock, prompting calls from President Isaac Herzog to avoid another election.
key_facts: Netanyahu's bloc leads with approximately 53 seats projected.
No coalition is expected to reach the majority of 61 seats.
President Herzog urges against a new election.

explore_lenses.label: What changed in the Knesset balance?
explore_lenses.title: Arab-led parties now hold the pivotal seats
explore_lenses.summary: The election did not produce a governing majority for either major Jewish-led bloc. The two Arab-led lists' combined result makes their parliamentary votes potentially decisive even though the leading blocs have said they will not enter a formal coalition with them.

claims.text: Final results reported by AP showed Netanyahu's bloc with 53 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc with 48, and the Joint List plus Ra'am with 19 in the 120-seat Knesset; 61 seats are needed for a majority.

The Joint List and Ra'am have ruled out a formal coalition with the Zionist opposition bloc, but officials have discussed tactical Knesset votes, including a possible vote to replace Speaker Amir Ohana.
Netanyahu's criticism appears aimed in part at discouraging Jewish opposition parties from relying on Arab-party votes in such parliamentary maneuvers.

explore_lenses.label: What evidence supports the interference claims?
explore_lenses.title: An inquiry exists; the allegations are unproven
explore_lenses.summary: The Central Elections Committee chair asked Shin Bet to examine suspicions of improper foreign influence, but that does not establish that Arab parties, foreign governments, or the overall vote count acted unlawfully. The reported inquiry is narrower than Netanyahu's public claim that the election was stolen.

claims.text: Central Elections Committee chair Justice Noam Sohlberg asked Shin Bet to investigate reported suspicions of improper foreign influence through funding; he said he could not attest to the substance of the suspicions.

Authorities had not publicly produced evidence substantiating Netanyahu's broader fraud allegations, and police and election officials said they had found no basis for claims of widespread or systematic voting irregularities.

Likud alleges that foreign-backed bribery and mobilization affected voting in Arab communities; Ra'am and the Joint List reject the accusations, while Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas has said he welcomes an investigation.
Qatar has categorically denied involvement in influencing the election.

explore_lenses.summary: The immediate contest is to assemble a 61-seat governing majority, while the election-interference inquiry continues. Reporting indicates the inquiry is not expected by itself to postpone the formation process or invalidate the reported result.

claims.text: The newly elected Knesset was due to be sworn in within 14 days of the October 27 election, according to reporting citing opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot.

AP reported that negotiations among the disparate parties could take weeks; if no bloc can assemble a majority, another election is a possible outcome.

story_report.summary: Israel’s election left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu without a parliamentary majority, after which he accused Arab Israeli parties of using foreign backing to influence the vote. Amid calls to investigate alleged vote buying, the Central Elections Committee chair asked Shin Bet to examine suspicions of improper foreign influence through funding, while saying he could not attest to their substance. Coalition negotiations are proceeding without a clear path to a governing majority.

sections.heading: Knesset Arithmetic Shapes Coalition Talks
sections.body: Final results reported by AP gave Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, against 48 for opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc and 19 for the Joint List and Ra’am; 61 seats are required for a majority. The two Arab party groupings have ruled out a formal coalition with the Zionist opposition, but officials have discussed tactical votes, including a possible effort to replace Speaker Amir Ohana. Reporting indicated Netanyahu’s criticism was aimed partly at deterring Jewish opposition parties from relying on Arab-party votes.

sections.heading: Foreign Influence Claims Face Scrutiny
sections.body: Likud has alleged that foreign-backed bribery and voter mobilization affected Arab communities, an accusation rejected by Ra’am and the Joint List. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas has said he welcomes an investigation, while Qatar has categorically denied trying to influence the election. Authorities had not publicly produced evidence supporting Netanyahu’s broader fraud allegations, and police and election officials said they had found no basis for widespread or systematic voting irregularities.

sections.heading: Herzog Faces Fragmented Government Formation
sections.body: The new Knesset was due to be sworn in within 14 days of the October 27 election. A Central Elections Committee source said the Shin Bet inquiry would not delay the publication of results or prevent President Isaac Herzog from selecting a party leader to begin coalition-building. Negotiations among the disparate parties could take weeks, and another election remains possible if no bloc can assemble a majority.

unresolved.text: It remains unknown whether tactical cooperation among opposition and Arab parties could develop into a stable governing arrangement rather than produce only isolated Knesset votes.
The inquiry’s evidence, scope and possible legal consequences have not been made public, so no conclusion can yet be drawn about foreign interference or any effect on seat allocation.
It is not yet known whom President Herzog will ask to form a government or whether either leading candidate can secure sufficient outside support.

related_stories.title: Pope Leo XIV Makes History as First Pontiff to Vote in a U.S. Election
related_stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a U.S. election, casting a mail-in ballot for the upcoming midterm elections. The Vatican confirmed that the Chicago-born pontiff exercised his right as a U.S. citizen by submitting his vote from Vatican City. The specific details of his ballot, including his choice of candidates, have not been disclosed.

related_stories.title: Humanitarian Evacuations Begin in Oleshky Amid Severe Shortages
related_stories.summary: Evacuations of residents from Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine, commenced on October 30 as part of a joint relief operation involving both sides. This marks the first such operation in nearly five years of conflict. The area has faced dire food and medical shortages, prompting the urgent need for humanitarian assistance.
